title: Lok Sabha Speaker Recognizes Shiv Sena Merger, Weighs TMC Rebels Ahead of Monsoon Session
excerpt: Speaker Om Birla approved the merger of six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs into Eknath Shinde's faction while the request by 20 TMC rebels to join the NCPI remains under consideration, reshaping parliamentary dynamics before the session opens July 20.
body:
• Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has approved the merger of six Shiv Sena (UBT) rebel MPs with the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena, reducing Uddhav Thackeray's Lok Sabha strength to just three MPs.
  • Twenty rebel Trinamool Congress MPs who sought to merge with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) have their request still under consideration, with Union Minister Kiren Rijiju confirming the matter is before the Speaker.
  • The decisions come days before the Monsoon Session opens on July 20, fundamentally altering opposition numbers and boosting the NDA's parliamentary strength.
  • Both the TMC and Shiv Sena (UBT) have demanded disqualification of the rebels under the anti-defection law, arguing that individual MPs cannot merge with another party — only the original party can.

Speaker Approves Shiv Sena Merger

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has formally recognized the merger of six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs with the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena faction, dealing a devastating blow to Uddhav Thackeray's political standing in Parliament just days before the Monsoon Session begins on July 20.

The six MPs — Sanjay Haribhau Jadhav, Bhausaheb Rajaram Wakchaure, Omprakash Bhupalsingh Nimbalkar, Sanjay Dina Patil, Sanjay Uttamrao Deshmukh, and Nagesh Bapurao Patil Ashtikar — had formally crossed over to the Shinde faction on June 22 in what was dubbed "Operation Tiger," the second major split in Shiv Sena in four years.

The approval leaves Shiv Sena (UBT) with just three Lok Sabha MPs — Arvind Sawant, Anil Desai, and Rajabhau Waje — down from nine elected in 2024. The party may also lose its Parliament office, since only parties with five or more MPs are entitled to office space in the complex.

"According to the anti-defection law, only a party can merge with another party; members can't go and merge with a party. We have asked the Speaker that those MPs cannot be recognised."

— Arvind Sawant, Shiv Sena (UBT) MP

TMC Rebels Still in Limbo

The larger and more politically consequential decision — whether to recognize the merger of 20 rebel TMC MPs with the little-known Nationalist Citizens Party of India — remains pending. Union Minister Kiren Rijiju confirmed on Friday that the request is under the Speaker's active consideration.

Led by Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, the 20 TMC lawmakers broke away from the party in June and announced their merger with the NCPI, a registered but unrecognized party headquartered in Howrah, West Bengal. The group includes prominent names such as former Union Minister Sudip Bandyopadhyay, actress-turned-politician Satabdi Roy, and former cricketer Yusuf Pathan.

TMC Lok Sabha leader Abhishek Banerjee has submitted 20 separate petitions demanding the rebels' disqualification. He argued that the anti-defection law's Tenth Schedule does not permit individual members to form a group and merge with another party — only the original political party can initiate a merger.

If the Speaker accepts the merger, the NCPI would instantly become the second-largest NDA constituent in the Lok Sabha with 20 MPs, surpassing both the TDP (16 MPs) and the JD(U) (12 MPs).

The Legal Battle Over the Tenth Schedule

Both cases hinge on a contested reading of the anti-defection law's merger provisions. The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution provides that defection does not apply when two-thirds of a party's legislators merge with another party. But critics — including both the TMC and Shiv Sena (UBT) — argue that this provision applies only to the party itself, not to individual members forming a separate group.

Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Anil Desai made this argument directly to the Speaker, stating that "any group of a legislature party cannot merge into some other party on its own, even if they have a two-thirds majority."

In the Shiv Sena case, six of nine MPs — exactly two-thirds — switched sides, meeting the numerical threshold. The TMC rebels represent 20 of 28 remaining MPs (one TMC MP has died), also exceeding the two-thirds mark.

The Speaker consulted legal and constitutional experts and examined past precedents before reaching his decisions, according to parliamentary sources.

What It Means for the Monsoon Session

The combined effect of both decisions, if the TMC merger is also approved, would dramatically strengthen the ruling NDA's numbers heading into what is expected to be a contentious Monsoon Session. The DMK has separately sought new seating arrangements away from Congress after the principal opposition party broke its decades-old alliance with the Tamil Nadu party.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with political roots in Maharashtra and West Bengal, the realignment carries deep significance. The Shiv Sena split — the second since the 2022 crisis that brought down the Maha Vikas Aghadi government — continues to reshape the political landscape of Maharashtra. The TMC rebellion, meanwhile, has upended West Bengal's political equations following the party's losses in the 2026 state elections.

With the Monsoon Session opening in two days, the Speaker's decisions will set the stage for what promises to be one of the most politically charged parliamentary sessions in recent memory.
